beats.headline: How does a single thread serve 100K ops/sec?
beats.subline: Redis bypasses disk locks and thread context switches entirely.
beats.narration: Your SQL database stalls on disk I/O and locks. Redis handles hundreds of thousands of operations per second on a single command thread. Let's look inside its event loop.

beats.title: Redis Single-Threaded Event Loop
beats.subtitle: Non-blocking socket I/O feeds sequential RAM operations

nodes.label: epoll / kqueue
nodes.detail: OS Multiplexing reads buffers into memory

nodes.label: Single Event Loop
nodes.detail: Executes commands sequentially with zero locks

nodes.label: RAM Data Structures
nodes.detail: Listpacks, skip lists & dicts in RAM

beats.narration: Linux epoll monitors thousands of client sockets simultaneously. Socket buffers read concurrently, but command execution stays single-threaded. By running strictly in RAM, Redis updates data in nanoseconds without lock contention.

beats.title: The Lethal O(N) KEYS Command Trap
beats.caption: Never run KEYS * in production environments!

lines.text: --> Blocks event loop for 4.2 seconds! All clients timeout.

beats.narration: Because command execution is single-threaded, running KEYS star scans millions of items and freezes the event loop. Every other service timing out waiting for simple reads. Always use non-blocking cursor SCAN in production.

beats.title: String JSON vs Redis Hashes

top.label: Full JSON Serialized String
points: Must rewrite entire 1KB JSON for 1 field change
Heavy serialization overhead on Java app

bottom.label: Native Redis Hash
bottom.code:
HSET user:1001 tier "GOLD"
HINCRBY user:1001 logins 1
points: Updates fields atomically on the server

beats.narration: Storing full JSON strings requires downloading and reserializing the entire blob just to bump a counter. Redis hashes let you update individual fields directly on the server with compact listpack memory efficiency.

beats.title: Part 1 Locked In
takeaways: epoll I/O multiplexing handles high socket concurrency
O(N) commands like KEYS block single-threaded event loop
Hashes enable field updates without full JSON rewrite

beats.narration: That's the RAM event loop. In Part 2, we dive into RDB snapshotting, AOF logs, and why background forks can crash your host with out-of-memory errors.

beats.headline: Snapshotting can trigger Linux OOM kills!
beats.subline: Setting maxmemory to 80% RAM leaves zero room for Copy-On-Write forks.
beats.narration: Your Redis memory usage looks completely safe until a background persistence rewrite fires during peak traffic. Suddenly the Linux kernel kills your primary process.

beats.title: Copy-On-Write (COW) Memory Fork
beats.subtitle: Parent serves writes while child serializes memory snapshot

nodes.label: Parent Redis Process
nodes.detail: Serves live client traffic during snapshot

nodes.label: fork() System Call
nodes.detail: Spawns child sharing identical RAM page table

nodes.label: Child Snapshot Writer
nodes.detail: Writes RDB binary file from static page table

beats.narration: When saving snapshots, Redis calls fork to create a child process sharing memory pages. But when client writes arrive, Linux duplicates modified pages using Copy-On-Write. Heavy writes can double your memory consumption instantly.

beats.title: Production redis.conf Persistence Guardrails
beats.caption: Hybrid RDB preamble with safe memory limits

lines.text: # Keep RAM cap at 65-70% total memory for COW headroom
# Hybrid persistence: fast RDB header + 1s AOF log

beats.narration: Configure maxmemory to roughly seventy percent of physical system RAM. Combine appendfsync everysec with aof-use-rdb-preamble yes to get lightning fast restarts with a strict one second durability window.

beats.title: Eviction Policies: LRU vs LFU

top.label: allkeys-lru (Least Recently Used)
points: A sudden SCAN burst can wipe out popular keys

bottom.label: allkeys-lfu (Least Frequently Used)
points: Tracks access frequency counters over time
Protects hot catalog items during bulk scans

beats.narration: Least Recently Used evicts items based solely on timestamp, meaning batch scans can evict your hottest cache items. Least Frequently Used tracks access frequency, keeping popular products in RAM regardless of batch reads.

beats.title: Part 2 Complete
takeaways: Reserve 30% RAM headroom for Copy-On-Write background forks
aof-use-rdb-preamble combines fast startup with AOF durability
LFU policy prevents cache pollution from sudden scan bursts

parts.partTitle: Sentinel, Cluster & The Hash Tag Trick

beats.headline: Multi-key commands fail in Redis Cluster!
beats.subline: Keys on different primary nodes cannot execute together without Hash Tags.
beats.narration: You move from single-instance Redis to a distributed Cluster, and suddenly your multi-key batch reads start throwing CROSSSLOT errors. Here is why it happens and how curly braces fix it.

beats.title: 16,384 Hash Slot Distribution
beats.subtitle: Keys map to primary nodes via CRC16 modulo 16384
beats.narration: Redis Cluster splits data into 16,384 logical hash slots distributed across primary nodes. Smart Java clients compute the CRC16 hash of the key to talk directly to the correct primary node without proxy hops.

beats.title: Fixing CROSSSLOT Errors with Hash Tags
beats.caption: Curly braces force related keys into the same hash slot

lines.text: (error) CROSSSLOT Keys in request don't hash to the same slot

beats.narration: Multi-key operations like MGET or Lua scripts require all target keys to sit inside the same hash slot. By wrapping user ID 1001 in curly braces, Redis hashes only that tag, forcing both keys onto the exact same shard.

beats.title: Sentinel HA vs Redis Cluster Sharding

top.label: Redis Sentinel
points: Automatic failover for single primary instance
Dataset size bounded by single machine RAM

bottom.label: Redis Cluster
points: Scales RAM and write throughput across nodes
Uses Hash Slots & smart client redirection

beats.narration: Sentinel provides failover for a single primary, but your dataset cannot exceed one machine's RAM. Redis Cluster shards data horizontally across multiple nodes, giving you practically unlimited memory and write capacity.

beats.title: Part 3 Complete
takeaways: Redis Cluster divides keyspace into 16,384 hash slots
Curly braces {tag} force keys onto same cluster shard
Sentinel provides HA failover; Cluster provides scaling

beats.headline: Default Spring Redis serialization corrupts inspection!
beats.subline: JDK serialization writes binary junk that ruins redis-cli and causes class bugs.
beats.narration: If you use default Spring Data Redis configuration, your keys and values become unreadable binary blobs in CLI, creating security vulnerabilities and deployment failures. Here is the enterprise bean setup.

beats.title: Configuring RedisCacheManager JSON Serialization

steps.explanation: Uses UTF-8 strings for clean key naming and redis-cli visibility.
Replaces unsafe JDK binary serialization with clean human-readable JSON payloads.
Prevents infinite cache accumulation by forcing strict 15-minute expirations.

beats.narration: Always configure explicit String key serializers and Jackson JSON value serializers. This makes key data readable in terminal commands, avoids class versioning issues, and enforces a fallback fifteen minute expiration.

beats.title: Atomic Rate Limiter with StringRedisTemplate

steps.explanation: Atomic server-side INCR command prevents race conditions across instances.
Sets 60-second expiration window only when counter key is created.

beats.narration: For custom logic like rate limiting, inject StringRedisTemplate. Atomic increment operations execute directly on the Redis server without client locks, and we set a sliding one-minute expiration on key creation.

beats.title: Deleting Big Keys Without Blocking
beats.caption: UNLINK frees memory asynchronously on background threads

lines.text: # Scanning whole keyspace for big keys...

beats.narration: Never call DEL on a key containing millions of elements because memory deallocation blocks the single thread. Use UNLINK instead to reclaim RAM asynchronously in a background thread.

beats.title: Level 7 Redis Mastered!
takeaways: Configure Jackson JSON & String serializers for Redis
Use StringRedisTemplate for atomic INCR & ZSET operations
Use UNLINK instead of DEL to remove big keys asynchronously
